Week 2 · GEOG 4/594 · Junjie Chen, PhD, PH · junchen@pdx.edu

Slide 1 Oregon Lakeshed Terrain Roughness

  • Terrain and hydrologic analysis for lakeshed delineation, and an investigation of the relationships between precipitation, stream system density and terrain roughness.
  • Example graduate term project, March 2017

Slide 2 Research Question

  • What are the relationships between Oregon lakeshed terrain roughness, stream drainage system density, and rainfall averages?

Slide 3 Datasets Used

  • NHDPlus - flow, flowlines, lakes, waterbodies
  • NHD / PNW Hydrography for Oregon Subwatershed boundaries
  • State Boundary for mask
  • Mosaic to new raster 10m DEM for Oregon (uoregon.edu)
  • NHD Catchments for lakeshed delineation
  • NHD Lake Spill Points
  • PSU CSAR Lakeshed Delineations

Slide 4 Delineating Oregon Lakesheds

Slide 5 Oregon Subwatershed Boundaries (up to 6th/7th level)

  • Main base for delineating lakesheds
  • Also used spill points
  • Nested hydrologic unit boundaries to the 6th level
  • Boundaries are defined by hydrographic and topographic criteria that delineate an area of land upstream from a specific point on a river, stream, or similar surface waters.

Slide 12 Terrain Preprocessing and Arc Hydro Analysis

  • DEM Reconditioning
  • Fill Sinks
  • Flow Direction
  • Flow Accumulation
  • Drainage Line
  • Drainage Density
  • Once drainage density is found, can be used for Basin Scale Ruggedness, or can be compared to TRI (Terrain Ruggedness Index)

Slide 13 Lakeshed Stream Drainage Density Results

Slide 14 Basin-Scale Ruggedness (Rb)

  • Simple mathematical index used to compare the relief of basins using streamlines and basin boundary polygons
  • Calculated Drainage Densities
  • Equation: Rb = Area Basin/DD
  • Again, mask raster analysis by lakeshed boundary
  • * I decided to use TRI in further analysis, as I think it was a more accurate judge of surface “roughness”

Where Rb = basin ruggedness index, A = area of the lakeshed boundary, and DD = drainage density.

Slide 15 Terrain Roughness Index (TRI)

  • Mosaic to Raster for finer DEM
  • Output: 10m Oregon DEM
  • Focal Statistics (min, max)
  • Mask raster analysis by desired lakeshed boundary
  • Raster Calculator Equation: Riley Method / Classification
  • Suitable for Oregon??? IE Nellemann’s Classification for Brown Bears

TRI = SquareRoot(Abs(Square("3x3max") − Square("3x3min")))

Riley classTRI range (m)
Level0–80
Nearly level81–116
Slightly rugged117–161
Intermediately rugged162–239
Moderately rugged240–497
Highly rugged498–958
Extremely rugged959 and above

Slide 16 Riley Classification vs. Natural Breaks

  • Riley Method for TRI Makes Oregon look the way your mother likes it.

Slide 17 Lakeshed Ruggedness Results (TRI)

  • Set raster analysis extent to lakeshed in question
  • Make lake surface “no data”
  • Run focal statistics min, max
  • Run TRI in raster calculator
  • Result is TRI of land surface, without water surface
  • What’s important? Range, mode, mean? Depends on who cares.
  • Abert Lake lakeshed = “2” class

Slide 23 Did I Meet the Proposal Budget?

  • Hell no.
  • I will be going over, unless I figure out a faster method.

Slide 24 Further Research Goals and Lessons Learned

  • Complete focal statistics and TRI before reprojecting!
  • Has to do with resampling errors….
  • Analyze every distinct lakeshed
  • Problem solve for lakesheds that need to be delineated yet
  • Increase productivity, perhaps coarse resolution
  • Lakesheds that go out of Oregon Boundary?
  • Thank You!
